cards.front: What is the event loop?
cards.meaning: How a single-threaded JS runtime decides what runs next after the current call stack empties. This unit is the scheduler; the host queues callbacks, and the loop picks them when the stack is empty.

cards.front: Event loop: three structures?
cards.meaning: Call stack (what is running right now — sync, LIFO), macrotask/task queue (timers, I/O, script turns, many host callbacks), microtask queue (Promise jobs, queueMicrotask, async/await continuations). Queues run only when the stack for the current turn is empty.

cards.front: How do Promises/async fit this unit?
cards.meaning: Here they matter only as queue citizens. Prerequisite is single-threaded JS (one stack; host queues callbacks). The Promises unit explains how jobs get into the microtask queue and how values/errors propagate.

cards.front: What is the call stack?
cards.meaning: It holds active function frames. The engine runs the top frame. Synchronous work pushes and pops frames until that turn of work is done. LIFO: last call on top.

cards.front: Can a queued callback start mid-function?
cards.meaning: No. Nothing from the queues starts mid-function unless that function schedules work and later returns — or hits await, which exits the current sync portion and schedules a continuation.

cards.front: When are queues eligible to run?
cards.meaning: Only when the stack for the current turn is empty. A busy stack delays timers, I/O callbacks, Promise reactions, and UI work — even if the host already finished waiting.

cards.front: Is the initial script a macrotask?
cards.meaning: Yes — the whole classic script/module evaluation turn is the initial macrotask. Sync logs and scheduling happen there before any queued callbacks.

cards.front: Is setTimeout delay exact?
cards.meaning: No — it is a minimum until the callback is eligible. The callback is still a macrotask; if the loop is busy (stack or microtasks), it runs later than the delay.
cards.notes: Common trap: treating the delay argument as exact.

cards.front: I/O callbacks and UI events — which queue?
cards.meaning: Macrotasks. I/O (network, disk) is host-dependent. UI events and rendering-related tasks are in the simplified browser model.

cards.front: setImmediate in the interview model?
cards.meaning: Node check-phase macrotask — not web standard. Don't memorize fragile order vs setTimeout(0); both defer after sync + microtasks. timeout vs immediate order can vary with timing.

cards.front: MessageChannel / postMessage scheduling trick?
cards.meaning: Sometimes used to schedule a macrotask sooner than timers. Still a macrotask, not a microtask.

cards.front: How many macrotasks run per cycle step?
cards.meaning: Pull one task, run it to completion (stack fills and empties). Then drain all microtasks before the next single macrotask.

cards.front: What schedules microtasks?
cards.meaning: promise.then/catch/finally (reaction jobs), queueMicrotask(fn) (explicit), await resume after the awaited value settles, MutationObserver callbacks (browser). process.nextTick is Node-only and runs even before ordinary microtasks.

cards.front: Why do microtasks exist as a priority?
cards.meaning: To finish related bookkeeping before yielding to timers, UI, or I/O. If every Promise.then waited behind every timer and paint, chains would feel randomly delayed.

cards.front: Why two queue priorities, not one?
cards.meaning: If Promise reactions waited behind every timer and paint, chains would feel randomly delayed. If everything were microtasks, a busy Promise chain could starve rendering forever — and that starvation is still possible if you abuse microtasks.

cards.front: Critical rule after each macrotask?
cards.meaning: Drain the entire microtask queue — including microtasks scheduled while draining — until empty, before the next macrotask (and before browser paint in the simplified model). That one fact resolves most predict-the-output questions.

cards.front: Event loop algorithm (memorize)?
cards.meaning: 1) Run the current sync script / current macrotask to completion. 2) Drain the entire microtask queue including new ones added while draining. 3) Browser: pending rendering/UI if it is time to paint. 4) Pull the next single macrotask. 5) Go back to step 2.

cards.front: Should you recite Node event-loop phases?
cards.meaning: Node's internal phases (timers, poll, check, …) are a finer map of macrotask kinds. For interviews, the microtask-vs-macrotask rule is the load-bearing model; mention Node phases only if asked.

cards.front: Sync; setTimeout(0); Promise.then chain; sync — order?
cards.meaning: 1 sync start, 5 sync end, 3 promise 1, 4 promise 2, 2 timeout. Whole script is the initial macrotask (logs 1, schedules timer, schedules first Promise microtask, logs 5). Then drain microtasks including the nested then; then the timer.

cards.front: Does a nested .then still beat the next timer?
cards.meaning: Yes. promise 1 runs as a microtask; its .then schedules promise 2 as another microtask; that still runs before any timer because draining includes microtasks added while draining.
cards.notes: Trap: ignoring nested .then and thinking the timer sneaks in between.

cards.front: Timeout A; Promise then B then C; timeout D; log E — order?
cards.meaning: E, B, C, A, D. Sync E first; then all microtasks from this turn (B then C, including the flattened inner Promise.resolve); both timeouts after those microtasks.
cards.example: setTimeout A; Promise.then { log B; return Promise.resolve(); }.then C; setTimeout D; log E → E B C A D

cards.front: Two setTimeout(0) in one script — order after microtasks?
cards.meaning: Both macrotasks queued in order during the script → A then D after all microtasks from that turn complete.

cards.front: async f: log f1; await null; log f2 — with sync caller?
cards.meaning: s1, f1, s2, f2. Code before the first await runs synchronously as part of the current turn; the rest is scheduled like a Promise.then (microtask) once the awaited value is settled. f2 loses to leftover sync (s2).
cards.example: log s1; f(); log s2 → s1, f1, s2, f2

cards.front: Does an await continuation beat setTimeout(0)?
cards.meaning: Yes. Continuations are microtasks, so they beat later setTimeout(0) macrotasks. Full Promise states belong in the Promises unit; the loop only cares that continuations are microtasks.

cards.front: Does await block the JS thread?
cards.meaning: No. It schedules a continuation and exits the current sync portion; other JS can run before resume. Thinking await blocks the thread is a common misconception.

cards.front: Can microtasks block setTimeout forever?
cards.meaning: Yes — if a microtask keeps scheduling more microtasks (e.g. a .then that recursively queues another .then), the queue never empties, so the loop never reaches the next macrotask or, in a browser, the next paint. UI looks frozen though timers are scheduled.
cards.example: function flood() { Promise.resolve().then(flood); } flood(); setTimeout(() => console.log('never'), 0);

cards.front: How do you avoid microtask starvation in practice?
cards.meaning: Prefer bounded work per turn. Don't implement tight loops only with Promise microtasks when UI responsiveness matters. Chunk CPU work across macrotasks — setTimeout(0), MessageChannel, requestAnimationFrame for frames — when you need to yield.

cards.front: process.nextTick vs Promise microtask (Node)?
cards.meaning: nextTick queue drains before ordinary Promise microtasks — Node-only, not web. Flooding nextTick starves I/O/timers even harder than Promise floods. Nest/Node interviews love this distinction.

cards.front: nextTick, Promise.then, setTimeout(0), setImmediate — typical order?
cards.meaning: Typical: nextTick, then promise. Then timeout vs immediate order can vary with timing. The stable teaching point is nextTick before promise — do not treat timeout vs immediate as a guaranteed order.
cards.example: setImmediate; setTimeout 0; Promise.then; nextTick → nextTick, promise, then timeout/immediate vary

cards.front: Should portable code use process.nextTick?
cards.meaning: No — it is not a web API. Prefer queueMicrotask or Promises for portable code. Know nextTick because Nest/Node interviews love it and because nextTick floods starve even sooner than Promise floods.

cards.front: Where does browser paint sit in the simplified model?
cards.meaning: Between macrotasks, browsers may paint when appropriate — after microtasks drain. Model: microtasks before paint opportunity before the next task. You don't need the full HTML event-loop spec.

cards.front: setTimeout(0) vs endless .then for yielding to paint?
cards.meaning: A microtask flood delays paint (starvation). Work scheduled only as setTimeout(0) yields more readily to rendering than endless .then chains.

cards.front: How to predict mixed async output?
cards.meaning: 1) Run all sync code in the current macrotask; note what gets queued where. 2) Drain all microtasks (and microtasks they spawn). 3) Run the oldest/next macrotask; repeat from step 2. Classify each callback as macrotask vs microtask (and nextTick before microtasks on Node).

cards.front: Classify setTimeout, setImmediate, then, queueMicrotask, await, nextTick?
cards.meaning: setTimeout/setInterval: macrotask. setImmediate (Node): macrotask (check). promise.then/catch/finally: microtask. queueMicrotask: microtask. await resume: microtask. process.nextTick: before microtasks (Node).

cards.front: After same sync turn: Promise.then vs setTimeout(0)?
cards.meaning: Promise microtasks always run before the next timer macrotask — common interview trap assuming setTimeout(0) runs first.

cards.front: Do microtasks run in parallel?
cards.meaning: No. Still one stack; they run one after another. Parallel JS is not how the queues work.

cards.front: Is Node's loop the same as the browser's?
cards.meaning: Do not assume Node === browser. process.nextTick and setImmediate are Node-specific. The shared interview model is still macrotask vs microtask drain-all.

cards.front: I/O finished vs callback ran?
cards.meaning: Host finishing only enqueues; the event loop decides when JS runs the callback — stack must be empty and scheduling rules satisfied.

cards.front: Closures vs event loop for a callback?
cards.meaning: Closures answer which variables a callback sees when it finally runs. The event loop answers when that callback is allowed to run.

cards.front: Event loop unit vs Promises unit?
cards.meaning: This unit is the scheduler (what runs next). The Promises unit explains how jobs get into the microtask queue and how values/errors propagate.

cards.front: What should you be able to draw/narrate?
cards.meaning: Draw stack + macrotask queue + microtask queue and narrate one full cycle; state drain-all-microtasks without hesitation; predict sync + setTimeout + Promise + chained .then; explain starvation and UI freeze; place await continuation in the microtask bucket; mention nextTick only as Node-before-microtasks when relevant.

cards.front: Strong event-loop closer (one-liner)?
cards.meaning: One task runs to completion; then every microtask — including ones scheduled during that drain — runs before the next timer or I/O task. That's why Promise callbacks beat setTimeout(0).
